name: Next-in-line effect
statement: People remember little of what was said just before their own turn to speak, because the coming performance takes the attention that encoding would have used.
meaning: The claim is about encoding, not about nerves in general. A person waiting to read, present or introduce themselves is still hearing what the previous speaker says, and later cannot report it. The measured quantity is recall or recognition for material as a function of its position relative to one's own turn, with the dip falling on the items immediately before that turn. Two accounts have been tested against each other. One puts the failure in a peripheral operation, such as breaking eye contact with the speaker. The other puts it in a central one, the elaborative rehearsal that turns a heard word into a retrievable memory. The evidence favours the central account, which is why the effect survives in settings where there is nobody to look at.

origin.where: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior
origin.note: Brenner's four-page paper "The next-in-line effect" named the phenomenon and supplied the turn-taking word-reading paradigm every later study modifies.

evidence: Brenner's own paper could not be obtained for this entry, and what follows is his design as Forrin, Ralph, Dhaliwal, Smilek and MacLeod describe it in 2019. Participants sat in pairs around a table. One member of each pair was a reader and the other a listener, the readers took turns reading words aloud to the group, and after the words had gone round the table twice everyone recalled as many as they could. Two results came out. Readers remembered their own words better than words they had heard, and readers had worse recall for words read shortly before their own turn, starting three words earlier. Listeners, who never faced a turn, showed no such dip. Brenner read this as anticipation competing for the attention that encoding needed. A conference paper by Ovid Tzeng in 1974 ran the same idea with sentences: 45 undergraduates in three groups of 15 sat in a circle and took turns reading a sentence card aloud, and recall peaked for the sentence a student read and fell for sentences two positions before to one position after it. Tzeng reports a figure rather than a test statistic. The sharpest numbers in the classic paradigm come from Adnan Omar and Charles Bond's 1989 conference paper, which seated 96 Texas Christian University students at 24 numbered desks over four sessions and had half of each group read words aloud in a predictable order. Splitting participants at the median of the Social Anxiety Scale, high-anxiety readers recalled 10.6% of words at the position before their turn against 25.7% at positions two to six back, F(1, 46) = 11.90, p < .001. Low-anxiety readers recalled 23.3% against 26.5%, F(1, 48) = 0.46, not significant.

replication.headline: Independent laboratories have found the pre-performance dip repeatedly since 1973, including in a 2019 recognition study of 100 people and a 2021 classroom study of 240.
replication.detail: Forrin and colleagues rebuilt the effect inside a single-participant memory task in 2019. Their Experiment 3 gave 100 Waterloo undergraduates a marker showing whether each upcoming word was to be read aloud or silently. Recognition of silent words was worse when an aloud word came next, F(1, 99) = 12.90, MSE = 0.02, p = .001, partial eta squared = .12, with d = 0.25 where the previous word was aloud and d = 0.26 where it was silent. Experiment 1, which used the same task without the markers, produced no positional effect, which is what the authors predicted: with no way to see the turn coming, anticipation sits flat across the whole list. Experiment 4 repeated Experiment 3 with the experimenter out of the room and 100 fresh participants, and the gap fell to one percentage point, t(99) = 0.87, p = .38, d = .08, with a Bayesian approximation giving positive support for the null at pBIC = .87. Caron, Hicks, Browne, Smilek and Forrin then took it to a simulated classroom in 2021. Their 240 undergraduates were told privately that they would present second, fifth, or not at all, and were quizzed on a confederate's opening presentation. Both groups expecting to present scored below those who were not, and second differed little from fifth. Silaban and colleagues repeated that design over Zoom in 2024 with 69 Indonesian students, where the control group's mean recognition score was 4.32 against 3.23 for those awaiting their turn, Mann-Whitney p = .011.

study.cite: Forrin, N. D., Ralph, B. C. W., Dhaliwal, N. K., Smilek, D., & MacLeod, C. M. (2019). Wait for it…performance anticipation reduces recognition memory. Journal of Memory and Language, 109, 104050.

limits: The effect has conditions attached, and every one of them was found by the people testing it. Innes reported in 1982 that readers lost recall against listeners when the words were loosely related, and that the difference was small when the words were strongly associated. Omar and Bond's deficit in 1989 was carried by the half of their sample scoring above the median in social anxiety, and their low-anxiety half showed nothing. Forrin's Experiment 4 lost the effect once the experimenter left the room, and the authors offer two readings of that null: the social presence was doing the work, or participants simply read aloud less often when unobserved. Bond, Pitre and van Leeuwen removed the effect in 1991 by instructing people to elaborate on what they heard, and Bond removed it in 1985 by telling people beforehand to make a special effort, which reversed the deficit into superior pre-performance recall. Sample sizes in the older work are small by current standards, and the two studies with the most legible numbers here, Tzeng and Omar and Bond, are unpublished conference papers held by ERIC rather than peer-reviewed articles. The searches behind this entry covered Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar's list of 63 papers citing Brenner, the Internet Archive's full-text index and web searches for preregistered or multi-laboratory attempts. No meta-analysis and no registered replication turned up. A search of PsycINFO, ProQuest dissertations or the Open Science Framework could find work these did not reach.
misreadings: The effect is often told as stage fright wiping out memory, which is close but points at the wrong step. Bond showed in 1985 that semantic cues at test do not shrink the deficit, and that instructions given before the words do, so the material was never encoded rather than being encoded and lost. Bond, Pitre and van Leeuwen then split the encoding account in two and found that verbal elaboration removed the effect while eye contact did not, placing the failure at elaborative rehearsal. Anxiety belongs in the story as a moderator: Omar and Bond found the deficit among socially anxious readers and not among the rest. A second confusion is with the spotlight effect, which this atlas holds separately at entry 22. That is a claim about overestimating how much others notice you. This is a claim about your own memory, and the two share only the fact that an audience is present. The reach of the dip is also reported inconsistently in later accounts, from three words before a turn to a window running from two items before to one item after, and Brenner's own figures were not available to settle it.
